A hook is an event, some conditions, an action, and a verdict Claude Code has to obey. In the next five minutes you'll install the signed host, scaffold a project, write a hook that blocks a dangerous command, and watch its inline tests pass.

## 1. Install the signed host

captain-hook dispatches through one fixed, signed application on macOS 15 or newer:

```bash
brew install --cask yasyf/tap/captain-hook
```

The cask installs `/Applications/Captain Hook.app`. The helper embedded in that exact path owns
the per-user host and its Python workers. There is no unsigned or project-local daemon and
no cold fallback when the host is missing.

## 2. Scaffold

From your repo root:

```bash
uvx capt-hook init
```

`init` creates `.claude/hooks/` with a starter hook, wires Claude Code's settings to dispatch every hook event through the signed host, and registers the plugin so the authoring skills load from it (nothing is copied into your repo). Prefer `uv tool install capt-hook` if you want the bare `capt-hook` on your PATH, or `uv add capt-hook` only if you're consuming it as a library — every command here uses the `uvx` form.

The app is the version authority: every event runs the exact `capt-hook` build the installed
host names, and the host upgrades itself in the background when a new release ships — the wheel
and app cannot drift apart. captain-hook never substitutes an older protocol, starts a private
daemon, or reruns the event cold.

## 3. Read a hook

`init` scaffolds `.claude/hooks/example.py` with a tour of the primitives — skim it later. First, the shape of a hook, using the gate from the front page:

<!-- gd-embed-fragment: canonical_hook -->

Read it top to bottom: the event is the agent trying to finish, `only_if` scopes it to sessions that touched UI files, `skip_if` stands it down once a visual review happened, and the message is what the agent sees when the gate holds.

## 4. Write your own

Create `.claude/hooks/safety.py`:

```python
# .claude/hooks/safety.py
from captain_hook import Allow, Block, Input, block_command

block_command(
    ["git", "push", "--force"],
    reason="Force-pushing rewrites shared history",
    hint="Use `git push --force-with-lease` instead",
    tests={
        Input(command="git push --force"): Block(),
        Input(command="git push origin main"): Allow(),
    },
)
```

One declaration, and the block covers the whole command family — chained after `&&`, buried in a pipeline, even mentioned in quotes. The `tests` dict is the hook's contract: each `Input` is a synthetic event, each value the verdict you expect.

## 5. Test it

```bash
uvx capt-hook test
```

```
PASS  safety.py::block_command  git push --force → Block
PASS  safety.py::block_command  git push origin main → Allow
5 tests: 5 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors, 0 skipped
```

That's the whole loop: declare, test, done. The next `git push --force` an agent attempts dies at `PreToolUse` with your reason and hint; LLM-backed hooks run their tests against recorded verdicts the same way.
